en: Compiled by the National Preceptor of the Chen and Sui Dynasties, the Great Master Zhizhe.
33. The First Gate of the Four Noble Truths, Part Three: 1. The Noble Truth of Suffering 2.
The Noble Truth of the Accumulation [of Suffering] 3. The Noble Truth of Cessation 4. The Noble Truth of the Path
Next, regarding the transcendence and the exposition of the Four Noble Truths:
this refers solely to what has been explained above concerning the various untainted (anāsrava) dhyānas.
Now, each of these dhyānas possesses the wisdom of contemplating the Four Noble Truths.
Having clarified the characteristics of dhyāna,
it conceals the underlying principle while manifesting the phenomenal events.
One establishes a name based on one's practice;
therefore, although there is the contemplation of the Four Truths,
the name is not derived from those truths.
It is like a treasure within a bag that is not extracted and shown to others;
thus, no one sees it.
For this reason,
following the various dhyānas,
I shall now further clarify the eight categories of dharmas concerning the practice of wisdom, such as the Four Noble Truths.
These four are collectively termed "truths" (*satya*).
"Truth" takes the meaning of being examined and verified as its definition.
This is the Dharma-gate of the Four Truths.
Since it is precisely for the sake of śrāvakas that understanding arises from hearing,
one must necessarily rely on the teachings to elucidate the principle;
now, it is clarified that the teachings and the principle are not in vain.
Therefore, it is said that one must examine the reality.
If a fruit is produced by means of a cause,
then the cause should necessarily precede the fruit.
That all [teachings] now present the effect first and the cause afterward is for the sake of convenience in guiding sentient beings through the gates of instruction; therefore,
they all present the effect first and the cause afterward.
First, the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). "Suffering" takes the sense of oppression and affliction as its meaning.
All conditioned mental formations are constantly oppressed and afflicted by the calamities of impermanence.
Therefore, it is called suffering.
There are three kinds of suffering:
first, the suffering of suffering (duḥkha-duḥkhatā).
Second is the suffering of change;
third is the suffering of conditioned formations.
Now, these three types of suffering are explained.
There are both specific and general [classifications].
The specific refers to the three types of suffering, which correspond specifically to the three types of sensation (*vedanā*).
The sensation of suffering arises from conditions that produce suffering.
The feeling of pain is suffering;
this is the suffering of suffering.
As for pleasant feeling:
When pleasure perishes, suffering arises;
this is precisely the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkha*).
As for neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*aduḥkhāsukhavedanā*), [it is also suffering].
That which is constantly subject to the shifting and movement of impermanence is precisely the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*).
If one discusses the three types of suffering comprehensively:
Thus, the three types of sensation (vedanā) universally comprise the three kinds of suffering.
The reason for this is that the mind of these three sensations—
This is precisely suffering,
because it arises universally from the conditions of suffering;
thus, it is universally suffering.
The mind of the three types of sensation is universally characterized by the aspect of disintegration;
because it is that which is disintegrated, it is universally the suffering of change (vipariṇāma-duḥkha).
The mind of the three types of sensation is universally characterized by the constant arising of activity and movement; therefore,
it is universally the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Whether it be the three types of feeling or the mind itself,
whether individually or collectively,
there is nothing that is not suffering.
One should know that suffering exists as something verified and real;
therefore, it is called a "truth" (*satya*).
Second, the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*): "origination" has the meaning of gathering and accumulating.
If the mind is associated with fetters and karma,
it will certainly bring about and accumulate the suffering of birth and death in the future; therefore,
it is called "accumulation" (samudaya).
The accumulation has three types of karma that encompass all karma:
first, unwholesome karma.
These are the ten unwholesome actions.
Second, the wholesome karmas;
these are the ten wholesome actions.
The three types of immovable karma are precisely the twelve gates of dhyāna,
as fully explained in the preceding analysis.
Regarding afflictions (*kleśa*):
two types of afflictions encompass all afflictions.
The first is the class of afflictions belonging to craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
The second category consists of afflictions belonging to views (*dṛṣṭi*).
These two types of afflictions give rise to all three poisons and the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*).
The ten proclivities (*anuśaya*),
the ninety-eight afflictions (*kleśa*), and so forth,
are all as previously explained.
If these afflictions combine with prior karma,
they will certainly bring about and accumulate the fruits of suffering— birth and death within the three realms— in the future;
this is precisely the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya).
Third, the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*): Cessation takes the sense of the unconditioned (*asamskrta*) as its meaning.
Once karma and the fetters are exhausted, there is no longer the affliction of birth and death.
Therefore, it is called "cessation.
If one gives rise to the true, untainted illumination that perceives and contemplates,
and severs the fetters through the thirty-four moments of mind, [this is so].
Then the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) of the three realms are all extinguished.
Because the fetters and proclivities of affliction are extinguished,
the karma of the three realms is also extinguished.
If the karma and afflictions of the three realms are extinguished,
this is the truth of cessation, which is nirvana with remainder.
Because the cause is extinguished, the fruit is extinguished.
When this retribution body is cast off,
the bitter fruits of future lives will never again continue.
This is called entering nirvana without remainder;
it is true extinction.
The principle of cessation is not empty.
Therefore, they are called truths (*satya*).
Fourth, the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*): "Path" has the meaning of being able to lead through.
It consists of the right path and the factors conducive to the path.
These two support one another and can lead directly to Nirvana;
therefore, they are called the Path.
As for the Right Path:
One truly contemplates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment,
the three gates of liberation,
and the practice of wisdom that takes principle as its object.
This is called the Right Path.
Next, the categories shall be set forth below.
As for the "Aids to the Path":
Within the contemplation of understanding,
one attains various methods of counteractive treatment as well as various meditative concentrations.
All of these are aids to the path,
as detailed above.
Furthermore, as for the "right path":
This refers to the sixteen moments of mind consisting of the eight patiences and eight knowledges of the vision of the truths;
and the eighteen moments of mind consisting of the nine non-obstructive paths and nine liberations of the path of cultivation.
It is true, untainted wisdom.
This is called the Right Path;
all other skillful means, antidotes,
meditative absorptions, and samādhis are secondary.
Furthermore, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment,
the three gates of liberation, and so forth,
are all aids to the path.
These two paths support one another and are able to lead to Nirvana;
they are authentic and not false.

This is precisely what is called the Truth of the Path (mārga-satya). 34. The First Gate of the Sixteen Aspects (ṣoḍaśākāra): Chapter Thirty-Four. The four aspects under the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya): 1. Impermanence (anitya) 2. Suffering (duḥkha) 3. Emptiness (śūnya) 4. Non-self (anātman) The four aspects under the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya): 1. Origination (samudaya) 2. Cause (hetu) 3. Condition (pratyaya) 4. Arising (jāti) The four aspects under the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya): 1. Exhaustion (kṣaya) 2. Cessation (nirodha) 3. Sublimity (praṇīta) 4. Detachment (niḥsaraṇa) The four aspects under the Truth of the Path (mārga-satya): 1. Path (mārga) 2. Rightness (nyāya) 3. Track (pratipad) 4. Vehicle (yāna) The sixteen aspects are thus explained in succession according to the Four Noble Truths.
Furthermore, one may separate the Four Noble Truths into sixteen aspects. However,
because the teaching methods possess the distinction between the general and the specific,
there is a difference in whether the Truths are treated as distinct or combined.
In order that those who practice contemplation may grasp the principles without error,
each of the Four Truths is subsequently analyzed according to four aspects.
Thus, the meaning and intent of "thoroughly examining reality" become even more clear and penetrating; furthermore,
this applies to those who practice and those who seek renown.
"Going" has the meaning of proceeding toward;
by practicing these sixteen methods of contemplation,
one is able to proceed toward the principle of the four realities.
Therefore, it is called "practice" (*caryā*).
Alternatively, it may derive its name from principle;
this refers to the sixteen truths (*ṣoḍaśa-satya*).
The four modes of contemplation under the Truth of Suffering: First,
the mode of impermanence consists of contemplating that the five aggregates of clinging arise from causes and conditions.
It arises and ceases moment by moment;
therefore, it is impermanent.
Second, it is suffering.
Contemplate the five aggregates of clinging:
if they are impermanent, they are suffering,
for they are oppressed by impermanence.
The practitioner of the three emptinesses contemplates the five aggregates of clinging as being without either a single characteristic or diverse characteristics.
Emptiness is itself emptiness.
Regarding the four kinds of selflessness:
one contemplates within the five aggregates of clinging.
The dharmas of "self" and "what belongs to self" are unattainable;
therefore, they are signless.
This is the practice of non-self.
The four aspects under the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*): First, regarding the aspect of origination (*samudaya-ākāra*),
one contemplates that the outflows (*āsrava*) and accumulations (*upacaya*) of the afflictions (*kleśa*) combine to bring about the fruit of suffering.
Therefore, it is called "practice of accumulation.
Second, as for the "practice of causes," one contemplates how the six causes give rise to the fruit of suffering.
Therefore, it is called "practice of causes.
Third, regarding the "practice of conditions":
because one contemplates that the fruit of suffering arises from the four conditions, it is called the "practice of conditions."
Regarding the "formations of birth" (*jāti-saṃskāra*):
because one again receives the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of a subsequent existence,
they are called formations of birth.
The four aspects under the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*): First, the aspect of exhaustion (*kṣaya-ākāra*).
One observes that various forms of suffering have been exhausted within nirvāṇa; therefore, it is called "exhaustion.
Second, the aspect of cessation (*nirodha-ākāra*).
Regarding the contemplation of nirvāṇa: it is called "cessation" because all fires of the afflictions have been extinguished.
Regarding the three sublime practices:
they are called "sublime" because nirvāṇa is the foremost among all things.
Fourth, regarding the practitioner who goes forth:
because they contemplate nirvāṇa as being apart from the worldly phenomena of birth and death,
it is called "going forth."
The Four Modes of the Truth of the Path: First,
the practitioner of the path contemplates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and so forth— the five aggregates not subject to grasping—
which are capable of leading one through to nirvana.
This is called the Path.
Second, regarding right practice:
it consists of contemplating the five aggregates of non-clinging, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and other such paths.
It is called "right" because it is not a perverted dharma.
Regarding the practitioner of the three tracks:
they contemplate the path of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and so forth.
It is called a "trace" because it is the place where all the noble ones have gone.
Those who practice the four vehicles contemplate the path of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and so forth.
It can transport practitioners;
they will certainly reach the three liberations.
Because afflictions such as craving and views cannot obstruct it, it is called a "vehicle" (yāna).

35. The First Gate of the Two Emptinesses of Beings and Phenomena, Part Three. 1. Emptiness of Beings (pudgala-śūnyatā). 2. Emptiness of Phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā). Next, the two emptinesses of beings and phenomena are explained following the sixteen aspects of the Four Noble Truths.
This clearly explains that although it is said that śrāvakas enter the path through the gateways of the Tripiṭaka teachings,
regarding these Tripiṭaka gateways:
Since there are these two distinct types of emptiness,
one should know that the cultivation of the sixteen aspects of the Four Noble Truths must likewise have its distinctions.
Therefore, according to the Abhidharma (Vibhāṣā), one attains the Way by perceiving existence;
according to the Tattvasiddhi (Satyasiddhi), one becomes a sage by realizing emptiness.
All of these differences arise from the distinct approaches of the two teachings on emptiness;
I shall now distinguish them for you.
Because the cultivation of the sixteen aspects of the Four Noble Truths differs,
the two types of emptiness— of phenomena (*dharma*) and of persons (*pudgala*)— are subsequently distinguished.
To speak of "emptiness" in general:
Emptiness has "non-existence" as its meaning.
Because these two types of existence— the existence of birth and the existence of phenomena—
do not exist, it is called empty.
First, the emptiness of sentient beings: if one contemplates the fruit of suffering in birth and death,
one sees only name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and the real dharmas of the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu).
Arising from causes and conditions,
they arise and perish moment by moment;
these are empty of intrinsic nature within the ultimate reality.
There is no self, person, sentient being, or life-span,
nor the sixteen views;
they are ultimately unobtainable, like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit.
This is the emptiness of sentient beings (*sattva-śūnyatā*).
Second is the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*): if one contemplates the fruit of suffering in birth and death, it is not only the self, persons, and sentient beings that are empty.
The sixteen modes of perception are empty,
like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit, which cannot be found. Within this,
there are the distinct dharmas of name, form, the aggregates, the bases, and the elements.
Distinguish each part individually;
analyze and break it down down to the level of atoms and moments,
examining each minute portion in detail.
That all things are entirely empty and non-existent is precisely what is called the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*).
This constitutes the explanation of the characteristics of the emptiness of phenomena for the śrāvaka practitioner.
If one discerns the emptiness of phenomena within the Mahāyāna,
all dharmas are like dreams and illusions;
they are empty by their very nature from the beginning.
It is not empty because of analytical deconstruction. 36. The Initial Gateway of the Thirty-Seven Factors of Enlightenment (Saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ).

Chapter Thirty-Six: Combining seven categories of dharmas to form the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment: 1. The four foundations of mindfulness; 2. The four right efforts; 3. The four bases of power; 4. The five faculties; 5. The five powers; 6. The seven factors of awakening; 7. The eightfold noble path. Regarding the subsequent arising of dharmas, these two types of emptiness are used to elucidate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
If one enters the Path by contemplating the two kinds of emptiness,
one must thoroughly understand the stages of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).
If one studies the noble path according to the gate of existence (*sattvadvāra*), [one must likewise understand these stages].
One must necessarily rely on the contemplation of the emptiness of sentient beings to cultivate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;
if one employs equanimity to sever delusions, [this is achieved].
Thus, one should pass through the emptiness of phenomena and practice within the gateway of the factors of enlightenment;
for this reason, it is explained next after the two types of emptiness.
Regarding the "Chapter on the Path" (Mārgavarga):
the meaning of "path" is as explained previously;
"chapter" (varga) refers to a category or class.
These seven categories of dharma-gates are all classifications according to the varying depths of entry into the Path; therefore,
they are called the "factors of enlightenment" (bodhipakṣa-dharmas).

The Four Foundations of Mindfulness: 1. The Foundation of Mindfulness of the Body 2. The Foundation of Mindfulness of Feelings 3. The Foundation of Mindfulness of the Mind 4. The Foundation of Mindfulness of Phenomena Regarding the Foundation of Mindfulness of the Body: it consists of six parts, beginning with the head.
The four great elements and the five sense faculties are a provisional combination;
therefore, it is called the "body.
Within this, the wisdom that contemplates the body constitutes mindfulness.
Clearly seeing the five kinds of impurity within one's own body destroys the inversion of regarding it as pure;
this is the [first] station. Observing the external body and both the internal and external bodies is likewise.
This is the foundation of mindfulness of the body.
Second, regarding the foundation of mindfulness of feelings: six feelings arise with the six contacts as their condition;
from these six feelings, three types of feeling arise.
This is called "feeling" (vedanā).
The wisdom that contemplates this feeling is called "mindfulness.
It clearly understands that all three types of feeling are suffering.
This is the point for destroying the perversion regarding pleasure.
One contemplates external feelings, and internal-external feelings in the same way.
This is the foundation of mindfulness of feelings.
Regarding the foundation of mindfulness of the mind: the six consciousnesses are able to cognize various objects and engage in conceptualization and grasping.
This is called the mind.
Within this, the wisdom that contemplates the internal mind is termed mindfulness.
One thoroughly understands that the mind arises from conditions,
does not abide for even a single moment,
and undergoes arising and ceasing in every thought-instant.
To destroy the perversion of permanence is precisely the locus.
Contemplating the external mind and the internal-external mind is likewise so.
This is the application of mindfulness to the mind.

As for the four applications of mindfulness to phenomena (dharma-smṛtyupasthāna): they consist of the two aggregates of perception and formations, as well as the three unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma).
This is called "dharmas.
Among these, the wisdom that contemplates dharmas is called "mindfulness" (smṛti).
It is the thorough penetration of all dharmas as being devoid of self or what belongs to a self.
Because they are ultimately unobtainable, there is no self; this is the destruction of the inversion of self.
This is the locus.
Contemplating external phenomena and both internal and external phenomena is likewise so.
This is the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
If the foundations of mindfulness are explained in the Śrāvaka sūtras,
they merely state that the destruction of the four inversions constitutes the foundations of mindfulness.
If the Mahāyāna elucidates the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna),
it explains that they constitute the destruction of the eight inversions.
This is what is meant by the foundations of mindfulness.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "If one can deeply contemplate the four foundations of mindfulness, this constitutes sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Regarding the four right efforts: first, to eliminate and sever unwholesome states that have already arisen."
1. With single-minded diligence and vigor, one does not allow unarisen unwholesome states to arise.
2. With single-minded diligence and vigor, one causes unarisen wholesome states to arise. 3. With single-minded diligence and vigor, one causes arisen wholesome states to increase.
4. With single-minded diligence and vigor, one maintains arisen wholesome states so that they do not decline.
With single-minded diligence and vigor,
one strives to abandon unwholesome states that have already arisen;
with single-minded diligence and vigor, one practices the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness.
If a mind of indolence arises,
when the mind is shrouded by the five hindrances and other afflictions,
and one is separated from the five kinds of wholesome roots beginning with faith.
If such evils as these have already arisen, one should apply oneself with single-minded diligence and vigor in order to sever them;
through skillful means, one eliminates and eradicates them until they are exhausted.
Second, one does not allow unarisen unwholesome states to arise.
When practicing the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness with single-minded diligence and vigor,
if a mind of indolence arises—
Furthermore, although the five hindrances and other such afflictions and unwholesome dharmas have not yet arisen, one fears they may arise later;
these obstruct the five kinds of wholesome roots, such as faith.
Now, for the purpose of preventing them from arising, [one applies effort].
With single-minded diligence and vigor,
one employs skillful means to prevent [unwholesome states] from arising.
Third, for the sake of producing wholesome dharmas not yet arisen.
When practicing the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness with single-minded diligence and vigor,
one acts so that the five kinds of wholesome roots, such as faith,
which have not yet arisen may arise.
With single-minded diligence and vigor,
one employs skillful means to practice so that wholesome roots such as faith may arise.
Fourth, for the purpose of increasing wholesome dharmas already arisen.
With single-minded diligence and vigor, when one practices the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness,
the five kinds of wholesome roots, such as faith and so forth, have already arisen;
for the purpose of causing them to increase, [one should apply oneself].
With single-minded diligence and vigor,
employ skillful means to cultivate the roots of goodness such as faith, ensuring they do not decline or be lost,
but rather increase and reach fulfillment.
These four are collectively termed "right efforts" because they destroy wrong paths and [establish one] within the right path.
Because they involve diligent practice, they are called the Right Efforts (*samyak-pradhāna*).

The Four Bases of Psychic Power (*ṛddhipāda*) are: first, the base of psychic power consisting of desire; second, the base of psychic power consisting of energy; third, the base of psychic power consisting of mind; and fourth, the base of psychic power consisting of investigation.
First, the basis of psychic power consisting of desire: with desire as the primary factor, one attains concentration,
accomplishes the formative forces of abandonment,
and cultivates the factors of psychic power.
This is the basis of psychic power consisting of desire.
Second is the basis of psychic power consisting of energy: having energy as the primary factor, one attains concentration and achieves the accomplishment of the formations of abandonment.
Cultivating the factor of concentration (*samādhi-aṅga*):
this constitutes the basis of psychic power consisting in energy (*vīrya-ṛddhipāda*).
Regarding the three bases of psychic power consisting in mind (*citta-ṛddhipāda*): with the mind as the primary factor, one attains meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Accomplishing the formative acts of abandonment, one cultivates the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
Regarding the four bases of psychic power through contemplation: by taking contemplation as primary, one attains meditative concentration.
Having accomplished the formative acts of abandonment,
one cultivates the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
Regarding these, they are generally termed "psychic" (*ṛddhi*).
Within the four foundations of mindfulness, there is true wisdom;
within the four right efforts, there is correct diligence.
Thus, diligence and wisdom increase.
The power of concentration is slight and weak because he has attained only the four types of dhyāna for the purpose of collecting the mind;
his wisdom and concentration are therefore equal.
Because all that is wished for is attained,
they are called the bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*).
They consist of wisdom, concentration, effort, and so forth.
Because they are able to sever the fetters and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), it is said that "the accomplishment of the applications of energy" (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*) is achieved.

The Five Faculties (*pañcendriya*): 1. The faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*). 2. The faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*). 3. The faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*). 4. The faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*). 5. The faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*). Regarding the first, the faculty of faith: it is faith in the Noble Path and the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
This is called the faculty of faith.
Second is the faculty of energy: when practicing the right path and all the wholesome dharmas that assist the path.
To seek with tireless diligence is called the faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*).
Third, the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*): to be mindful of the right path and all the wholesome dharmas that assist the path.
To have no other thoughts whatsoever is called the faculty of mindfulness (smṛtīndriya).
Fourth, the faculty of concentration (samādhīndriya): it consists of gathering the mind within the characteristics of the right path and the various wholesome dharmas that assist the path.
Non-distraction is the faculty of concentration.
The five faculties of wisdom constitute the Noble Path and all the wholesome dharmas that assist the path.
Contemplating the sixteen aspects, such as impermanence and so forth,
is called the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*).
These five are collectively termed "faculties" (*indriya*) because—
It is capable of producing [results].
Once the practitioner has attained the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*),
their wisdom and concentration become stable and secure.
That is to say, the five kinds of wholesome dharmas, beginning with faith—
whether they be semblances or actualities—
arise spontaneously.
For example, when the yin and yang are in harmonious balance,
all seeds will sprout and take root.

Therefore, they are called faculties (*indriya*). The five powers (*bala*): first, the power of faith; second, the power of diligence; third, the power of mindfulness; fourth, the power of concentration; fifth, the power of wisdom. Regarding the first, the power of faith: it is when one has faith in the right path and all the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).
If the faculty of faith increases, it can obstruct doubt and confusion,
and destroy all wrong beliefs as well as the afflictions;
therefore, it is called the power of faith.
Second is the power of diligence (*vīryabala*). When practicing the true path and its various auxiliary factors (*pakṣadharma*),
if the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*) increases,
one destroys the various forms of physical and mental indolence.
To accomplish supramundane matters is the power of diligence.
Third, the power of mindfulness:
when one recollects the right path and the various factors conducive to enlightenment.
If the faculty of mindfulness increases,
it destroys all wrong mindfulness and accomplishes all supramundane merits of right mindfulness. This is it.
It is the power of mindfulness.

Regarding the four powers of concentration: when the mind is gathered upon the right path and the various factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), if the faculty of concentration increases.
Thus one is able to destroy all distracted thoughts and give rise to the meditative concentrations (dhyāna) of both phenomena and principle;
this is called the power of concentration.
The five powers of wisdom serve as the right path and its various auxiliary factors.
When one contemplates the sixteen aspects of impermanence,
if the faculty of wisdom increases, [it becomes the power of wisdom].
Thus, it can obstruct the delusions of views and afflictions within the three realms and give rise to true outflow-free wisdom; therefore,
it is called the power of wisdom.
These five supernormal powers (abhijñā) are called "powers" because they can destroy all tainted (sāsrava) unwholesome states and accomplish supramundane wholesome deeds.

Therefore, it is called "power. The Seven Factors of Enlightenment (saptabodhyaṅga): 1. The factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena (dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga); 2. The factor of enlightenment of energy (vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga); 3. The factor of enlightenment of joy (prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga); 4. The factor of enlightenment of tranquility (praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga); 5. The factor of enlightenment of equanimity (upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga); 6. The factor of enlightenment of concentration (samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga); 7. The factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga). Regarding the first, the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena: when wisdom contemplates all phenomena...
Because one is well able to discriminate between the true and the false,
and does not erroneously grasp at deceptive phenomena,
it is called the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Second, the awakening factor of diligence (*vīrya-sambodhyaṅga*): When practicing the various dharmas of the Path with diligence,
one is able to discern them correctly and not engage in fruitless asceticism.
Constantly and diligently abiding the mind within practice of the true Dharma is therefore called the awakening factor of diligence (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Third, the awakening factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*): if the mind attains the joy of the Dharma...
One is well able to discern that this joy does not arise based on inverted dharmas,
but dwells with rapture in true dharma-joy; therefore,
it is called the factor of awakening of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
The fourth awakening factor, *prahāṇa-saṃbodhyaṅga*: when one eliminates the afflictions of various views,
one is skillfully able to discern and remove all falsehoods without damaging the true and genuine roots of goodness.
Therefore, it is called the awakening factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Fifth, the awakening factor of equanimity: when one relinquishes objects of attachment that have been perceived, one is skillfully able to clearly comprehend the objects thus relinquished.
To never again recollect what is false and unreal is the factor of enlightenment of equanimity.
The sixth is the awakening factor of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*). When entering various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*),
one is skillfully able to discern that these concentrations are empty and illusory,
so that views, attachments, and deluded thoughts do not arise.
This is the factor of enlightenment of concentration.
Regarding the seven factors of enlightenment: when practicing the supramundane path, one skillfully awakens to and maintains the equilibrium of concentration and wisdom.
If the mind becomes sunken,
one should attend to the factors of awakening— discrimination of phenomena, energy, and joy—
and investigate their arising.
If the mind becomes agitated,
one should apply mindfulness to eliminate it through the three factors of concentration (*samādhi*) and so forth. Therefore,
the factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is always present between these two extremes.
Equilibrium and appropriateness constitute the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness.
These seven are collectively termed "factors of enlightenment" (bodhyaṅga).
The seven factors of realization of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) lead to true awakening;
therefore, they are collectively termed "factors of awakening" (*bodhyaṅga*).

The eightfold noble path consists of: (1) right view, (2) right intention, (3) right speech, (4) right action, (5) right livelihood, (6) right effort, (7) right mindfulness, and (8) right concentration. Regarding (1) right view: it is when one cultivates the sixteen aspects of the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Seeing the Four Truths clearly and distinctly is therefore called Right View.
Second, Right Thought: at the time of seeing the Four Truths...
Associated with the untainted mind,
it is stirred by reflection,
characterized by awareness, and involves deliberation.
Because it causes [the mind] to increase toward entry into nirvana, it is called right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*).
Third, right speech (*samyag-vāc*): by means of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*).
Excluding the four kinds of wrong livelihood,
it encompasses verbal action and abides within all right speech;
this is right speech.
The four right actions: by means of untainted wisdom,
one eliminates all wrong bodily actions and abides in pure, right bodily action.
This is called right action (*samyak-karmānta*).
Regarding the five forms of right livelihood (*pañca-samyag-ājīva*):
by means of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*), one thoroughly eliminates the five types of wrong livelihood (*mithyā-ājīva*) among the three types of action.
To abide in pure and right livelihood—
this is right livelihood.
What are its five kinds?
First, for the sake of gain and offerings,
they falsely manifest extraordinary signs and wonders.
Second, for the sake of gain and offerings...
They speak of their own merits for three reasons: first, for the sake of gain and offerings; second, for the sake of gain and offerings;
and third, by divining omens of good and ill fortune, they preach the Dharma to others.
Fourth, for the sake of gain and offerings,
he raises his voice and displays an air of majesty to cause others to feel awe and respect.
Fifth, for the sake of gain and offerings...
They proclaim the offerings they have received to stir the hearts of others,
thereby sustaining their lives through improper causes and conditions.
Therefore, this constitutes wrong livelihood.
Sixth, right effort: being conjoined with untainted wisdom, one diligently exerts effort to cultivate the path to nirvāṇa.
This is right effort. Regarding the seven factors of right mindfulness:
they consist of mindfulness associated with untainted wisdom, recollecting the noble path and the factors conducive to enlightenment.
Therefore, it is called right mindfulness.
As for the eightfold right concentration: because one enters meditative absorption in association with untainted wisdom, it is called right concentration.
These eight are collectively termed the "Right Path" (*samyak-mārga*).
"Right" (*samyak*) has the meaning of being non-deviant.
Now, these eight factors do not proceed by relying on partiality or deviance.
All are termed "right" (*samyak*).
Because they can lead one through to *nirvāṇa*, they are termed the "Path" (*mārga*).

37. The Three Gates of Liberation. The Thirty-Seventh [Chapter]: The Three Gates of Liberation. First, the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*); second, the gate of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*); third, the gate of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*). Next are the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharmāḥ*).
Regarding the exposition of the three gates of liberation,
the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment..."
This is the practice of the path leading to nirvāṇa;
this path has already reached nirvāṇa.
The city of nirvāṇa has three gates.
That is to say, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Since the path has already been explained,
one should next explain the gateways to the attainment of the goal.
These three are called "gateways to liberation" (*vimokṣamukha*).
Liberation is itself the gateway to nirvāṇa;
that is to say, they are able to lead one through these three dharmas.
Those who are able to practice this path can enter nirvana; therefore,
it is called a gate of liberation.
They are also called the three samādhis.
The meaning of *samādhi* is as previously explained;
however, in this case, the term *samādhi* is named after its own essential nature.
Liberation is designated by the term "feeling" because it functions as the capacity for penetration;
there is no separate dharma apart from this.
A certain master explains it thus:
during the causal stage it is called samādhi,
while upon the realization of the fruit, its name changes to liberation (vimukti).
This category is like the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*) or the eight stages of release (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*).
First is the liberation door of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣa-mukha*). What is called the liberation door of emptiness?
It is the observation that all phenomena (*dharma*) are empty because they lack a self (*ātman*) or anything belonging to a self (*ātmīya*).
Why is this so? All phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions;
there is no creator.
There is no recipient.
One who can thus penetrate this is said to have the gate of liberation of emptiness.
This is the gate of liberation of emptiness.
It takes two aspects as its object:
namely, emptiness and selflessness.
Second is the gate of liberation through signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*). What is meant by the gate of liberation through signlessness?
It is the contemplation of the signs of male and female, as well as the signs of identity, difference, and so forth.
When one seeks reality within these marks, none can be found;
therefore, they are markless. Why is this so?
If all phenomena are empty because they lack a self or what belongs to a self,
then because they are empty, there is no male or female,
nor any phenomena such as identity or difference.
Within "self" and "what belongs to self," the names are distinct;
for this reason [they are different].
Characteristics such as the identity or difference between male and female cannot be found in reality.
One who can thus penetrate this understanding—
This is the liberation door of signlessness.
This liberation has four aspects as its conditions:
namely, exhaustion, cessation, excellence, and emergence.
The third is the gate of liberation through non-action (*asaṃskāra-vimokṣamukha*). What is meant by the gate of liberation through non-action?
It is when one knows that all phenomena are signless (*animitta*), such that there is absolutely nothing to be done.
This is called "non-action.
Why is this so? Because if one perceives anything as obtainable within phenomena, [it is not non-action].
Thus, within the three realms,
there arises aspiration and seeking;
because of this, one performs the karma that produces the three states of existence.
Now, because all marks are entirely unapprehendable,
one is thus [liberated] within the triple world.
There is no seeking or wishing;
one does not create any karma of birth and death within the three realms of existence.
Because there is no karma, there is no retribution.
This is the liberation door of wishlessness.
This liberation door of wishlessness takes the ten practices as its object.
That is to say: impermanence, suffering, the origin, and the causal conditions;
[and] the path, right progress, and the vehicle. Chapter 38:

The First Gate of the Three Roots of Non-outflow (Anāsrava-Indriya). 1. The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya); 2. The faculty of knowing (ājñendriya); 3. The faculty of one who has already known (ājñātāvīndriya). Next, the three roots of non-outflow are explained following the three gates of liberation.
Since liberation is the gateway to nirvana,
if one skillfully cultivates the three gates of liberation,
one will certainly give rise to true, untainted wisdom.
Regarding the realization of *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and the attainment of *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*,
there are three distinct paths.
This refers to the path of seeing, the path of cultivation,
and the path of no-more-learning.
It is at the time of realizing these three paths.
Because they necessarily give rise to the three faculties,
the next three liberations are explained [in this context].
They are collectively termed "faculties" (indriya) because—
The sense-faculties (*indriya*) have the meaning of being established through abiding and being capable of producing [their respective functions].
Having attained these three dharmas,
one abides firmly and does not regress.
Because it gives rise to the illumination of true wisdom,
it is called a faculty (*indriya*).
First is the faculty of "the unknown that one desires to know," which is a combination of the nine untainted (*anāsrava*) faculties.
For one who practices through faith and one who practices through the Dharma,
during the path of seeing the truths (darśanamārga),
these are termed the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya).
The so-called nine faculties are:

the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, the faculty of wisdom, the faculty of joy, the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of equanimity, and the faculty of mind.
Regarding the two faculties of knowledge: they pertain to those who have attained through faith-understanding and those who have attained through vision.
Within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*),
these nine faculties are designated as the faculty of knowledge (*ājñendriya*).
These nine faculties are to be distinguished as they were explained in the section on the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*).
Third, the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*): when one reaches the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*),
these nine faculties are transformed and are called the faculty of one who has already known.
The nine [faculties] are also to be distinguished as they were in the section on the faculty of "desiring to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya).

39. The First Gate of the Eleven Knowledges (ekādaśajñāna): 1. Knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) 2. Subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna) 3. Knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) 4. Conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) 5. Knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna) 6. Knowledge of origination (samudayajñāna) 7. Knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna) 8. Knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) 9. Knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) 10. Knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) 11. Knowledge of reality as it is (yathābhūtajñāna) Next, following the three untainted faculties (anāsravendriya), the eleven knowledges are explained.
Because the three faculties can give rise to eleven knowledges.
Why is this so? It is because of the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*).

One gives rise to the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna); one knows the arising of the faculties, as well as the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, the knowledge of cessation,
the knowledge of the path, the knowledge of others' minds, and conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna).
Having known this,
one gives rise to the knowledge of the destruction [of the outflows], the knowledge of non-arising,
and knowledge as it truly is.
For this reason, following the three faculties,
the eleven knowledges are distinguished.
They are collectively termed "knowledges" (jñāna) because they constitute decisive and definitive cognition.
Therefore, it is called "wisdom.
When these eleven types of wisdom arise,
each clearly illuminates its respective stage with distinct clarity.
Therefore, it is collectively termed "knowledge" (*jñāna*).

First, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*): this is the untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) regarding phenomena bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), and the untainted knowledge regarding the causes [of phenomena] bound to the desire realm.
The untainted knowledge within the cessation of the dharma-knowledge regarding the desire realm;
the untainted knowledge within the path for severing the factors bound to the desire realm;
and the untainted knowledge within the category of dharma-knowledge.
Second, subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*): Within the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*),
four types of untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) are distinguished according to the Four Noble Truths,
as also explained in the section on dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*).
There is only a distinction between those that possess [the knowledge of] dharmas and those that do not.

Third, the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*): it knows the present minds and mental factors (*caitta*) bound to the desire realm and the form realm, as well as a small portion of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) minds and mental factors.
This is the knowledge of others' minds.
Fourth, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*): all mundane, outflow-tainted wisdom is also called "knowledge of equality" (*samantajñāna*).
Both ordinary persons and noble ones possess this wisdom equally; therefore,
it is called "equalizing wisdom" (samvṛti-jñāna).
It is also called "knowledge of names.
This knowledge possesses only names but lacks underlying principles.
It is the "knowledge of the five sufferings," which occurs when one contemplates the five aggregates as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
One attains untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
Sixth is the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*): knowing the causes of all phenomena;
it is the contemplation of causes, origination, arising, and conditions.
It is untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
Seventh, the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*): it is untainted knowledge at the time of observing cessation, tranquility, excellence, and emergence.
The knowledge of the eightfold path (*mārgajñāna*) is untainted wisdom (*anāsravajñāna*) when one views the correct practice of the path from a distance.
The ninth is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*): "I have seen suffering, abandoned its origin, realized its cessation, and cultivated the path."
When one reflects in this manner,
untainted wisdom perceives clarity and awakening.
The ten knowledges of non-arising: "I have already seen suffering; I shall not see it again.
I have already abandoned the origin; I shall not abandon it again.
I have already realized cessation; I shall not realize it again."
Having already realized the path of cultivation, one no longer needs to realize it again;
having already cultivated it, one no longer needs to cultivate it again.
When one reflects in this way:
Taintless wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is vision, clarity, and awakening.
Eleventh is knowledge according to reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*): the general and specific characteristics of all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*).
Knowing things as they truly are with right wisdom,
without any obstruction—
this is called knowledge of reality as it is.
This wisdom exists solely within the mind of a Buddha; it is not possessed by those of the two vehicles. 40.

The First Gate of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, Number Forty-one: 1. Ignorance (avidyā), 2. Volitional formations (saṃskāra), 3. Consciousness (vijñāna), 4. Name-and-form (nāmarūpa), 5. The six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana), 6. Contact (sparśa), 7. Feeling (vedanā), 8. Craving (tṛṣṇā), 9. Grasping (upādāna), 10. Existence (bhava), 11. Birth (jāti), 12. Old age and death (jarāmaraṇa). Following the eleven types of wisdom, the twelve links of dependent origination are now explained.
Excluding the knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtajñāna*),
the remaining ten knowledges are all attained in common by the two vehicles.
For now, this has been explained briefly. As for śrāvakas,
it concerns only a single lifetime.
If one contemplates the Four Truths collectively and achieves only ten knowledges, then those knowledges are inferior; because the knowledges are inferior,
[the path is not supreme].
They are unable to eliminate the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*),
and their meritorious spiritual efficacy is likewise diminished.
This is the case for those who are *pratyekabuddhas*.
Comprehensively encompassing the three periods of time,
one minutely analyzes and contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination;
if one accomplishes the ten knowledges, then wisdom is powerful.
Because their wisdom is powerful,
they are able to erode and eliminate the habitual tendencies (vāsanā),
and their spiritual efficacy is likewise vast.
For this reason, the teaching of the Great Sage opened up a separate path for the Middle Vehicle;
such was his intention.
What is generally termed "conditioned origination" (pratītyasamutpāda) consists of these twelve factors,
which are able to produce results through their mutual interaction.
Therefore they are called causes (*hetu*).
Their existence is mutually dependent;
this is termed conditions (*pratyaya*).
When causes and conditions continue in succession,
the cycle of birth and death proceeds without end.
If one knows that ignorance does not give rise to grasping for existence, [the cycle ceases].
Then the cycle of birth and death within the twenty-five states of existence across the three realms will all cease;
this is the essential method for transcending the world.
Regarding the twelve links of dependent origination in the gateway of teaching:
There are three types of distinctions:
first, elucidating the twelve links of dependent origination in terms of the three periods of time;
second, analyzing the twelve links of dependent origination in terms of the two periods of retribution.
Third, the twelve links of dependent origination are explained in terms of a single thought-moment and a single lifetime.
Regarding the twelve links of the three times,
the first two are subsumed within the past life.
The latter two are subsumed within the future world;
the middle eight are subsumed within the present world.
Among these, three matters—afflictions, karma, and suffering—are briefly explained.
These three matters proceed in succession,
acting as mutual causes and conditions for one another;
they are the causes and conditions of afflictions and karma.
The causal conditions for the suffering of karma;
the causal conditions for the suffering of suffering; and the causal conditions for the suffering of afflictions.
The causal conditions of afflictions and karma;
the causal conditions of karma and suffering;
and the causal conditions of suffering and suffering.
This is what is meant by "successive progression," because they serve as mutual causes and conditions for one another;
thus it is called the twelve links of dependent origination throughout the three periods of time.
First, ignorance (*avidyā*): all afflictions of the past are collectively termed ignorance,
because in the past there was as yet no light of wisdom.
Because all afflictions arise from this, past afflictions are entirely ignorance.
Second, formations: karma arises from ignorance.
Karma is itself volitional formation (*saṃskāra*),
because wholesome and unwholesome karma can produce the fruits of the world.
Therefore, it is called "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*).
The three consciousnesses arise from volitional formations;
they produce a defiled mind, with the initial body as their cause, like a calf.
It is called "consciousness" (vijñāna) because it cognizes its own specific characteristics;
this occurs at the very moment of the parents' union.
The name for the time when one is about to enter the womb.
Fourth, "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*): the four non-material aggregates (*skandha*) arising from consciousness, together with the material aggregate that is received [in the womb];
this is called "name-and-form."
This is the name for the stage of *kalala*.
Regarding the six bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*): from within name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense faculties, such as the eye, arise.
This is called the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana).
From the moment the five blisters first open,
they are designated by the name "six sense bases."
The six contacts (*ṣaṭ-sparśa*): the conjunction of the sense bases, the objects, and consciousness is called contact.
This is because the six objects come into contact with the six faculties.
Thereupon the six consciousnesses arise;
thus it is called the conjunction of the sentient faculty, the object, and consciousness.
Seven: Feeling—feeling arises from contact.
Therefore, it is called "feeling" (vedanā).
This is due to the six types of contact (sparśa);
through the contact of the six sense faculties (indriya), one experiences the six objects (viṣaya).
These are the six types of feeling (*ṣaḍ-vedanā*).
Regarding the eight types of craving (*tṛṣṇā*): that which arises from within feeling and consists of mental attachment is called craving.
This refers to the arising of craving in the mind toward the six objects of sensory experience that have been perceived.
The nine appropriations are sought through the causal condition of craving.
This is called grasping (*upādāna*);
it refers to the seeking and seizing of desirable objects.
From grasping, the causes for karma in future lives are established.
This is called "existence" (bhava).
Because there can be a fruit due to a cause,
it is called "existence."
Eleventh, birth (*jāti*): from existence, one again receives the body of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) in a future life;
this is called birth.
That is to say, it refers to taking birth within the four modes of birth (*catasro yonayaḥ*) and the six destinies (*ṣadgati*).
Twelfth, old age and death: the maturation and decay of the body composed of the five aggregates arising from birth is what constitutes old age and death.
From old age and death, there arise sorrow, lamentation, and weeping.
Regarding the various sorrows and sufferings,
and the convergence of manifold afflictions:
if one correctly contemplates the pure true nature of all phenomena, [these will be extinguished].
Then ignorance is exhausted.
Because ignorance is exhausted, volitional formations are exhausted,
and so on until the entire mass of suffering is exhausted.
If one can thus correctly contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination throughout the three periods of time and give rise to true outflow-free wisdom.
One becomes a pratyekabuddha.
Next, it clarifies the observation of the characteristics of the twelve links of dependent origination from the perspective of retribution across two lifetimes.
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* has been fully expounded;
now, the scriptural text is briefly extracted.
This is the twelvefold chain of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).
Since ignorance is analyzed starting from the *kalala* stage,
it is called "fruition" (*vipāka*).
This is explained in terms of two lifetimes.
The first ten causes and conditions belong to the present;
the latter two causes and conditions belong to the future.
Taken together across these two periods, they constitute twelve.
First, regarding ignorance (*avidyā*):
The *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra* states, "What is meant by contemplating ignorance?
One first contemplates the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)."
Regarding the parents, a mind of lustful attachment arises;
due to the conditions of this craving, the four great elements combine,
forming two drops of semen and blood.
These combine into a single drop,
about the size of a bean,
which is called *kalala*.
This *kalala* has three factors:
first, life; second, consciousness; and third, warmth.
From within past lives...
In the causal retribution of karma,
there is neither an agent nor a recipient.
The initial inhalation and exhalation is called ignorance at the stage of the kalala.
Regarding the inhalation and exhalation of the breath,
there are two paths: namely,
following the upward and downward movement of the mother's breath.
It undergoes transformation once every seven days.
The inhalation and exhalation of breath is called "life-span";
this is termed the "pathway of wind."
It is neither putrid nor rotten;
this is called "Heat" (ūṣmagata).
Within this state, the mind and mental factors [are present].
This is called consciousness.
Good son, if there is one who wishes to attain the state of a pratyekabuddha,
they should contemplate these twelve links of dependent origination in this way.
The Second Practice: Furthermore, one contemplates the causes and conditions of the three types of sensation, as well as the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements.
How does one contemplate them?
Following the mind, one contemplates the inhalation and exhalation of the breath,
and observes the internal body— its skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, and brain—
as being like clouds in the sky.
The wind within this body is likewise:
there is a wind that can move upward.
There is a wind that can cause things to descend;
there is a wind that can cause them to fill;
there is a wind that can cause them to wither.
There is a wind that can cause increase;
therefore, the inhalation and exhalation of breath are called bodily formations (kāyasaṃskāra).
The breath arises from vitarka and vicāra;
therefore, it is called mental activity (manas-karman).
Through their conjunction, sound is produced.
This is called verbal activity.
Through the causal conditions of these three activities,
consciousness arises.
Therefore, it is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
Fourth is "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*): by reason of consciousness as its condition, there arise the four aggregates (*skandha*) as well as the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
Therefore it is called "name-and-form.
Regarding the "six sense bases": because the five aggregates, conditioned by consciousness, proceed toward the six locations, they are called the "six sense bases."
The six contacts: because the eye and visible forms encounter one another, it is called contact;
this extends up to the mind and mental phenomena.
It is also like this.
There are seven types of feeling (*vedanā*).
Because of the causal condition of contact (*sparśa*), the mindfulness of forms up to mental phenomena (*dharma*) is called feeling.
8. Craving (*tṛṣṇā*): This refers to the greedy attachment to form (*rūpa*) and so forth, up to mental phenomena (*dharma*).
This is called craving.
9. Grasping (*upādāna*): It arises with craving as its causal condition.
Because one seeks and pursues [objects] in the four directions, it is called "clinging" (upādāna).
There are ten types of clinging; by reason of these ten clingings, [existence arises].
Because one receives a subsequent body, it is called "existence" (bhava).
There are eleven types of existence; because they have causes and conditions, they exist.
Birth is what constitutes birth.
Due to the twelve links of old age and death, and because of birth as their causal condition,
there arise various forms of suffering, including old age and death.
This is called the great tree of the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, and the twelve links of dependent origination; these are all brief expositions from the sutras.
From the very first moment of receiving retribution...
The characteristics of the twelve links of dependent origination are clarified by way of two lifetimes;
there is not a single word here that is private or obscure.
Let the reader seek this well.
One should know that this differs from the previous explanation of the twelve links of dependent origination across the three periods of time.
Next, the twelve links of dependent origination within a single thought-moment are explained,
which are considered solely within the context of a single lifetime.
As soon as a single thought arises,
it is already complete with the twelve links of dependent origination;
this is also from the Mahāsannipāta Sūtra.
Now, I shall briefly extract from the sūtras the characteristics of the twelve links of dependent origination within a single thought-moment.
First is ignorance: when one sees forms with the eye and gives rise to a mind of attachment, this is ignorance.
Second, formations (*saṃskāra*): performing karma out of craving is what is called formations.
Third, consciousness (*vijñāna*): focusing the mind with single-minded attention.
Therefore, it is called "consciousness.
Fourth is "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa): consciousness together with form functions;
this is called name-and-form.
The six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana): craving arises from the six bases;
these are called the six sense bases.
The six contacts (ṣaṭsparśa): because of the sense bases, one seeks out craving.
This is called contact (sparśa).
As for the seven types of feeling (vedanā),
